items.actClause:
AN ACT to amend the general business law, in relation to restricting youth
sports operators and youth sports facilities from prohibiting parents and
guardians from taking in-person recordings or photographs of their children
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S8666

SPONSOR: MAY
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the general business law, in relation to restricting
youth sports operators and youth sports facilities from prohibiting
parents and guardians from taking in-person recordings or photographs of
their children

 
PURPOSE:

To protect the right of parents and guardians to take in-person photo-
graphs and video recordings of their own children at youth sports
events, while allowing reasonable, safety-based restrictions.

 
SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

This bill amends the General Business Law by adding a new Article 41-A
governing youth sports facilities and youth sports operators. The bill
prohibits such facilities and operators from banning or restricting
parents or guardians from taking in-person photographs or video
recordings of their own children during youth sports events.

Specifically, the bill prevents facilities and operators from requiring
parents to purchase photography or video services as a condition of
recording their child, conditioning a child's participation or a
parent's admission on waiving recording rights, or confiscating or disa-
bling personal recording devices. The bill allows reasonable, content-
neutral restrictions narrowly tailored to safety, preventing interfer-
ence with play, compliance with court orders or privacy laws, or
limiting access to restricted areas.

The bill also requires facilities and operators to post clear notice of
these rights and renders unenforceable any contract, waiver, or policy
that attempts to waive or restrict a parent's ability to record their
own child. The bill does not prohibit facilities from offering photogra-
phy or video services for sale, provided those services are not used to
limit parental rights.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

Parents and guardians routinely attend youth sports events to support
their children and to document important moments in their development.
In recent years, some youth sports facilities and operators have adopted
policies that prohibit or restrict parents from taking in-person photos
or videos of their own children, or that require parents to purchase
exclusive recording services to access footage.

These practices can be confusing, burdensome, and unfair to families.
They may also limit parents' ability to share memories, monitor their
child's experience, or maintain personal records of participation.  This
bill establishes a clear, statewide baseline that protects parental
rights while preserving the ability of facilities and operators to
impose reasonable safety-based rules.

By making these protections explicit and uniform, the bill provides
clarity for parents, facilities, and operators alike, and ensures that

families are not forced to surrender basic rights as a condition of
participation in youth sports.

 
LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

New bill.

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

None.

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
This act shall take effect on the ninetieth day after it shall have
become a law.

A.actClause:
AN ACT to amend the general business law, in relation to restricting youth
sports organizations and youth sports facilities from prohibiting attendees of
youth sports events from recording personal media
A.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S8666A

SPONSOR: MAY
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the general business law, in relation to restricting
youth sports organizations and youth sports facilities from prohibiting
attendees of youth sports events from recording personal media

 
PURPOSE:

To protect the ability of families and attendees to take personal photos
and videos at youth sports events, while maintaining reasonable, safe-
ty-based rules and transparency around commercial media services.

 
SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

This act adds a new Article 41-A to the General Business Law governing
youth sports organizations and youth sports facilities. It prohibits
organizations and facilities from banning, restricting, or penalizing
attendees for taking personal photos or videos at youth sports events
where spectators are permitted.

Organizations and facilities may not require the purchase of a photo or
video package as a condition of participation, entry, or attendance.
They are also barred from bundling media packages into registration or
other fees unless the cost is clearly and separately listed.

Where media packages are offered, organizations must clearly disclose
whether the package is optional, the full price, and the identity of the
vendor, including any relationship between the vendor and the organiza-
tion or facility.

Reasonable limits on recording are permitted in specific circumstances,
such as for safety, privacy, or in areas not open to the public. Any
such limits must be unrelated to commercial interests and must apply
equally to all attendees.  Organizations and facilities may continue to
enter into agreements with media companies to film or stream events, but
those agreements may not be used to prevent attendees from taking their
own photos or videos.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

Parents and families attend youth sports events to support their chil-
dren and to capture important moments. For many, these events are not
just games but milestones-first goals, final seasons, and shared experi-
ences that that families want to remember. The ability to take a photo
or short video from the stands has long been a normal and expected part
of that experience.

In recent years, some youth sports organizations and facilities have
adopted policies that restrict or discourage personal recording. In some
cases, families have been told they cannot take photos or videos at all.
In others, access to images or footage has been tied to the purchase of
a professional media package, sometimes bundled into registration or
event fees without clear notice. These practices can place families in a
position where they must pay to capture ordinary moments or risk penal-
ties for doing what has traditionally been allowed.

This act responds to those changes by establishing a clear baseline:
attendees at youth sports events may create personal media, and that
activity cannot be restricted or penalized for commercial reasons. At
the same time, it recognizes that youth sports settings require appro-
priate safeguards. Organizations and facilities may continue to enforce
reasonable rules to protect safety, preserve privacy, and maintain
order, including limits in non-public areas such as locker rooms.

The act also addresses the growing commercialization of youth sports
media. Photography and streaming services can provide value, but fami-
lies should not be required to purchase them or be misled about their
cost. By requiring clear disclosure of pricing, optionality, and vendor
relationships, the act ensures that families can make informed decisions
without hidden fees or pressure.

Importantly, the act preserves existing laws governing the use of a
minor's image and allows organizations to require parental consent for
official uses and to set reasonable rules for private or sensitive spac-
es. It also excludes school-based athletic programs and Olympic and
national governing body programs, where separate regulatory structures
already apply.

By setting clear, fair rules, this act preserves a common experience for
families, prevents coercive or unclear practices, and provides consist-
ency across youth sports programs in New York State.

 
LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

New bill.

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

None.

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
This act shall take effect on the ninetieth day after it shall have
become a law.

B.actClause:
AN ACT to amend the general business law, in relation to requirements of youth
sports organizations
B.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S8666B  
TITLE OF BILL:  An act to amend the general
SPONSOR: MAY
business law, in relation to requirements of youth sports organizations

 
PURPOSE:

The Love of the Game Act protects families in competitive youth sports
from hidden costs, coercive contracts, misuse of children's data, and
pay-to-record policies at games or sporting events.

 
SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

* Youth sports organizations must give families a written, itemized list
of all season costs and any withdrawal penalties before the season
starts. They cannot charge anything that was not disclosed.

* Contracts cannot require exclusivity, last more than one season, or
impose undisclosed penalties for leaving.

* Organizations cannot require families to use an affiliated hotel or
travel vendor, or penalize them for booking elsewhere.

* Families must receive a data bill of rights. Athletes' personal data
cannot be sold or used for targeted advertising, and families can have
it deleted.

* Parents can take photos and video at games. Organizations cannot
require families to buy media packages or hide their cost in other fees.

* Companies that control a youth sports organization are liable for its
violations. Families cannot be forced into arbitration.

* Families can sue for damages, and the Attorney General can seek penal-
ties and other court orders.

* School sports, Olympic and national governing body programs, and
organizations charging $100 or less per season are exempt.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

Youth sports should be about the love of the game. They teach children
discipline, teamwork, and perseverance, build friendships, and encourage
habits of physical activity that can last a lifetime. New York families
invest considerable time and money in these opportunities. They deserve
to know that their children's interests come before someone else's
profits.

Competitive youth sports have become a major commercial industry, with
private equity firms and other investors acquiring clubs, leagues, tour-
naments, and facilities. Investment can improve facilities and expand
opportunities, but it can also create pressure to extract more revenue
from families who have little bargaining power. Once a child joins a
team, walking away can mean losing far more than money.

Hidden fees are a common example. Families register at one price, only
to discover mandatory travel, tournament, uniform, or equipment charges
after their child has committed. This bill requires full disclosure of
costs before the season and prohibits undisclosed charges. It also

requires transparency about payments to affiliated vendors, so families
know where their money goes and who profits from it.

The same principle applies to so-called stay-to-play arrangements, which
force families to book through designated hotels or travel companies,
sometimes at inflated rates that benefit the organization.  Teams can
face penalties for refusing. A child's opportunity to compete should
never depend on which hotel their parents choose.

Restrictive contracts present another problem. Exclusivity provisions,
multi-season commitments, and unexpected withdrawal penalties can trap
young athletes in programs that no longer suit them. Children should be
free to change teams, explore another sport, or step away without unfair
financial consequences. The bill preserves reasonable protections for
organizations without allowing them to hold families captive.

Children's personal information also deserves protection. Registration
systems and player platforms collect performance metrics, health infor-
mation, location data, and household financial details. New York already
protects student information through requirements for schools and their
vendors. This bill extends comparable protections to private youth
sports organizations. Information collected to help children participate
should not become a product sold to advertisers.

Families should also retain the simple pleasure of recording their chil-
dren playing. Some organizations prohibit personal photography or video
to steer parents toward paid media packages. The bill protects recording
from the stands, subject to reasonable safety and privacy rules, while
ensuring that commercial photography and streaming services remain
optional and transparently priced.

Corporate accountability matters as well. Complex ownership structures
should not shield companies that control youth sports organizations and
profit from their operations. Under this bill, responsibility follows
control, including compliance with labor and child safety laws. Families
also retain their right to seek justice in court rather than being
forced into arbitration.

The bill gives families meaningful remedies when organizations violate
these protections and removes the financial incentive for misconduct.
It also allows courts to protect the continuity of a season when an
operator is held accountable, so children do not bear the consequences
of corporate wrongdoing.

Importantly, the bill excludes school athletics, Olympic and national
governing body programs with their own oversight, and community programs
charging $100 or less per season. Volunteer-rum local leagues face no
new obligations. The goal is not to burden the people who make youth
sports possible, but to hold accountable those who exploit families'
commitment to their children.  Kids should play for the love of the
game, not for someone else's love of profits. This bill makes sure the
business of youth sports serves the children and families who make it
possible.

LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:
2026: S8666A (May).  Also draws on 2026: S10428 (May).

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:
None to the state.

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
This act shall take effect on the ninetieth day after it shall have
become a law.

summary: Relates to requirements regarding athlete agreements with youth sports organizations, including disclosure of total annual costs; prohibits stay-to-play provisions; provides for athlete data privacy; prohibits youth sports organizations from restricting attendees from personal recording and photography; provides for investor liability, arbitration, and enforcement.
title: Relates to requirements of youth sports organizations
